source: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect
finding: Design. Students estimated factual quantities five times in a row. Pay was for accuracy only, with no reward for matching others. Three conditions: no information, the group arithmetic mean of the last round, or full information (all 12 trajectories).
numbers: N=144 ETH Zurich students, 12 sessions of 12, 6 Swiss-fact questions (e.g. murders 2006, true value 198). Pay 1.40/0.70/0.35 CHF for estimates within 10/20/40% of truth. 24 groups per condition.
limits: Student lab sample. Only bare numeric feedback, no discussion. Hard, right-skewed questions, so the result is tied to the log scale. Confidence was asked only after rounds 1 and 5.
agent_relevance: Any attempt that sees other attempts' numbers will shrink its spread. Supports G4/G9 (isolated attempts) as a design rule.

source: Lorenz et al. (2011) - the three effects
finding: Three claimed harms of mild influence: (1) social influence effect: group diversity falls with no gain in collective error; (2) range reduction effect: the truth moves to the edge of the estimate range; (3) confidence effect: people feel more sure with no accuracy gain.
numbers: Wisdom-of-crowd indicator (how many central estimates are needed to bracket the truth) was about 1 unit lower with information than in control; the drop was larger under aggregated than under full information. Confidence rise was significant in both information conditions vs control (regression with clustered SEs).
limits: Exact coefficients are in a figure, not in the text. The authors say effects were weaker for easier questions and more confident people (SI) and left this untested.
agent_relevance: Shared outputs make a crowd look tighter and surer than it is. Do not count agreement among attempts that saw each other as independent evidence.

source: Lorenz et al. (2011) - aggregation facts
finding: Raw first-round estimates are right-skewed. The arithmetic mean is a poor aggregate here; the geometric mean and the median work. So the wisdom of crowd shows only on the log scale.
numbers: Arithmetic mean closer to truth than individuals in only 21.3% of cases. In log space the mean beat individuals in 77.1%. Table 1: arithmetic mean error +1337% (population density) and +1357% (assaults); geometric mean errors -11.9% to -55.4%; median errors -0.7% to -60.9%.
limits: The 'no accuracy gain' claim uses log-transformed collective error, which is the authors' choice of measure.
agent_relevance: When attempts give numbers spanning orders of magnitude, aggregate with the median or the log-scale mean.

source: Lorenz et al. (2011) - diversity prediction theorem as the frame
finding: Average individual error equals collective error plus group diversity (squared error). Shrinking diversity lowers average individual error even if the crowd average does not move. Both sides of the debate use this identity.
numbers: Identity: (mean - truth)^2 + variance = mean of (x_i - truth)^2, applied to log(x/truth).
limits: The identity is exact but says nothing about whether a shift of the mean is toward the truth.
agent_relevance: Bookkeeping rule for any ensemble of attempts: diversity is the budget that aggregation spends.

source: Lorenz et al. (2011) - data cleaning and difficulty condition
finding: The authors say the effect needs questions of moderate difficulty: if people know the answer, copying cannot show. Leaders, persuasion and competition were left out on purpose.
numbers: 13 of 864 five-round runs (1.5%) hit the top pay band every round. Ten values removed: five from one person who mixed up metres and km, four 'fun moves', one zero.
limits: Limits generalisation to rich social settings.
agent_relevance: Boundary: if an attempt already has a verified answer, seeing others costs little; harm is largest at middle difficulty.

source: Farrell (2011) Social influence benefits the wisdom of individuals in the crowd
finding: Re-analysis of the Lorenz data. Shrinking toward the group helps individuals: they earn more reward and their confidence rise tracks that reward. The bracketing metric rewards high variance. Over-shrinkage is the open question.
numbers: Fig. 1 of the comment: mean reward per estimate is higher in the full and aggregate conditions after five rounds. No effect size in the text.
limits: A commentary on the original data, not a new experiment.
agent_relevance: Competing view: influence is useful shrinkage, like multilevel modelling. Isolation is a choice about the collective answer, not individual quality.

source: Rauhut, Lorenz, Schweitzer, Helbing (2011) Reply to Farrell
finding: Reply: better individual reward is expected from the diversity prediction theorem when collective error stays constant. The harm is at group level. The danger: an outsider sees a tight, confident group and trusts it. They call it collective tunnel vision.
numbers: No new data. Notes that rewards were shown only after confidence was reported.
limits: Concedes the individual-level gain. The dispute is about which level matters.
agent_relevance: Our final answer is a collective output of attempts, so the group level is the one that matters.

source: Mavrodiev, Tessone, Schweitzer (2013) Quantifying the effects of social influence
finding: Re-analysis of the aggregate-information condition. The change in a guess is linear in the distance to the previous group mean. This holds across questions whose answers differ by about 10 orders of magnitude.
numbers: Robust regression, 192 samples per question. Slope b1 by question: Q1 0.97, Q2 0.27, Q3 0.83, Q4 0.60, Q5 0.40, Q6 0.46 (all p<0.005).
limits: Fits only the mean-feedback condition. The slope varies about 3.5 times across questions, so the weight on others is not constant. Builds on French 1956 and DeGroot averaging.
agent_relevance: A simple baseline for how far an LLM attempt moves toward shown answers.

source: Bazazi, von Zimmermann, Bahrami, Richardson (2019) Self-serving incentives impair collective decisions by increasing conformity
finding: Pay by individual accuracy made people converge on the shown group mean. Pay by group accuracy kept diversity and accuracy. This is against the belief that individual incentives produce diverse thinking.
numbers: N=141 in 23 groups of 4-8 (70 individual pay, 71 collective pay), UCL. 16 'Where in London?' questions, 2x2: pay x social info (group mean shown as a star). Individual pay: diversity lower with info, MPE=99.88%; error higher, MPE=99.57%. Collective pay: diversity MPE=73.35%, error MPE=69.13% (little evidence of effect). Overall social-info effect: diversity MPE 95.85%, error 98.32%.
limits: Two responses per trial, one statistic shown (the mean), a spatial task, a university subject pool (94 female, mean age 25.4). Bayesian mixed models. The pay-scheme difference overall was weak (diversity MPE 76.25%, error 65.35%). No replication found.
agent_relevance: Reward design shapes copying. If attempts are scored on agreement with the pack we build herding pressure. Score attempts on checkable correctness (G4/G9).

source: Bazazi et al. (2019) - theory background
finding: Prediction-contest theory says relative-performance rewards make people discount public signals. Other theory says individual pay plus a minority bonus gives optimal diversity. Bazazi tests individual vs collective pay directly.
numbers: No numbers; cites management-science models.
limits: The authors note that the theory assumes independent opinions and ignores that people must see others to know the minority.
agent_relevance: Two incentive routes to diversity (rank-based or collective pay). Neither is a free fix.

source: Jayles et al. (2017) How social information can improve estimation accuracy in human groups
finding: Counter-evidence. Hard questions in France and Japan. Social influence improved collective accuracy (median of log estimates) when reliable virtual experts were planted. Log estimates are Cauchy-like, not Gaussian.
numbers: Median sensitivity to social influence S=0.34. Types: keep (S=0), adopt (S=1), compromise, overreact, contradict. Confident quarter: peak at S=0 about 7x the peak at S=1; followers: under 2x. S rises linearly up to about 2.5 orders of magnitude of distance. Virtual experts gave the true value at 0, 20, 43 or 80% of the sequence (n=0, 5, 15, 80 per 20 human participants).
limits: Sequential design with the geometric mean of previous answers as feedback. The gain comes from planted correct sources; at 0% experts collective performance did not improve.
agent_relevance: Influence from a reliable source helps. A verified signal (a test result) is a virtual expert; a peer attempt is not.

source: Jayles et al. (2017) - model and counter-bias result
finding: An agent model with sensitivity S, fitted to data, reproduces the distributions. It predicts that a moderate share of wrong information can offset the human tendency to underestimate quantities and improve the group.
numbers: Model simulates 20 sequential estimates per run over conditions (rho, tau).
limits: The prediction rests on a stable underestimation bias; it would not hold for an unbiased or overestimating crowd.
agent_relevance: The effect of shared information depends on the bias direction of the sources.

source: Jayles et al. (2020) The impact of incorrect social information on collective wisdom in human groups
finding: Planted wrong 'virtual influencers' did not wreck the crowd. Many people follow social information only partly. Incorrect information that pushed against the underestimation bias helped more than correct information.
numbers: 20 sessions of nine people; 32 questions answered twice; n = 0, 5 or 15 virtual influencers added to 20 human estimates; alpha in -2, -1, -0.5, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3 (distance from truth); tau = 1 or 3 shared estimates.
limits: Sequential design, so each person sees earlier people. Not the Lorenz full-information vs none contrast.
agent_relevance: Boundary on 'influence is bad': partial following gives robustness, as long as people weigh their own estimate (S below 1).

source: Jayles et al. (2021) Impact of sharing full versus averaged social information on social influence and estimation accuracy
finding: Sharing the full list or just the average gave comparable accuracy gains. People followed the average more, more so with a larger underlying count, and followed higher-than-own information more than lower.
numbers: Between-subject treatments Sorted, Unsorted, Aggregated; tau varies within groups. Estimates narrowed after sharing in all treatments. Collective accuracy improves 'albeit marginally'. S=1 at most 2% of cases at tau=1, none in Aggregated for tau>1.
limits: The text notes that individual accuracy can improve without collective accuracy if estimates converge with no median shift, as in Lorenz. Gains are small.
agent_relevance: Partial replication: narrowing is robust, the harm to accuracy is not. Format (mean vs list) matters less than expected.

source: Becker, Brackbill, Centola (2017) Network dynamics of social influence in the wisdom of crowds
finding: Boundary found by network structure. In decentralised networks of equal connectivity influence narrowed opinions and improved accuracy. In centralised networks error rose when the central node was off the truth.
numbers: N=1,360 web participants. Decentralised: SD of estimates down 43% (round 1 to 3, 13 trials, p<0.001); individual error down 23%; median error 0.76 to 0.67 SD (-12%); mean error 0.69 to 0.62 SD (-10%). Centralised: worse when the centre pointed away from truth (n=13, p<0.01). Revision size correlated with initial error: rho=0.41, 95% CI [0.39, 0.43], 4,340 estimates by 1,040 subjects.
limits: Paid for accuracy, 3 rounds. Improvement needs accurate people to hold more self-weight (DeGroot with unequal weights). Replicates the diversity drop (43%) but not the accuracy drop.
agent_relevance: Key boundary: who is the hub. A lead attempt that all others see acts as a bias source. Supports isolation (G4/G9) and warns against a lead-attempt design.

source: Becker, Porter, Centola (2019) The wisdom of partisan crowds
finding: Even on politically biased facts, peer exchange in same-party networks raised accuracy and cut polarisation. This contradicts the fear that homogeneous groups amplify bias.
numbers: Experiment 1: 12 social trials per party, 4 control. Error of the mean fell 35% from round 1 to 3 in social groups vs 15% in control (p<0.03). All 12 Republican and all 12 Democrat trials improved (p<0.001).
limits: Paid web samples, numeric factual questions, small number of trials. The control also improved a little (p<0.15).
agent_relevance: Same-bias peers still helped when truth was checkable and the network was decentralised. Do not assume all peer copying is harmful.

source: Kao et al. (2019) Modular structure within groups causes information loss but can improve decision accuracy
finding: Model of modular groups. Modular structure silences part of the group. That hurts in simple information environments but helps in complex ones where small groups are most accurate.
numbers: No human data. Information loss is detrimental in simple environments; in complex ones modularity improves accuracy since a large group behaves like a smaller one.
limits: Animal-collective model that assumes correlated information. Not LLM outputs.
agent_relevance: Partial isolation (sub-groups) could beat both full isolation and full sharing when evidence is correlated.

source: Strategies for integrating disparate social information (Proc R Soc B, 2020)
finding: People heed social information that confirms their own judgement; one confirming peer cuts the weight on more distant peers. Higher peer variance cuts impact. A Bayesian-plus-heuristics model fits the adjustments.
numbers: Abstract only read: three peers, variance and skewness varied. Exact N not recorded.
limits: Only the abstract was read, so no numbers were taken.
agent_relevance: Confirmation-weighted copying is a known human pattern. LLMs may share it.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Bastos, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Study 1: a crowd of 12 LLMs matched a human crowd on forecasting. Study 2: showing GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median improved their accuracy, but averaging human and machine forecasts beat that.
numbers: Study 1: 31 binary questions vs 925 human forecasters; LLM crowd Brier M=0.20 (SD 0.12); equivalent to the human crowd in an exploratory equivalence test. Acquiescence: mean prediction above 50%. Study 2: accuracy gain of 17% to 28% after seeing the human median.
limits: Older models (GPT-4, Claude 2). The influence is one trusted strong source, not peers. Study 2 does not measure diversity loss.
agent_relevance: A strong external signal helps LLMs. Averaging independent outputs afterwards is better than letting the model update toward them.

source: Barrera-Lemarchand, Sigman, Navajas (2026) The Wisdom of Artificial Deliberative Crowds
finding: Closest LLM test of Lorenz. Three small LLMs from different families (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5-nano, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite). Seeing each other's numbers improved accuracy over their own first answers, but deliberation did much better.
numbers: Study 1: 14 jar photos, 38 to 589 disks. Social influence vs own first answer: Wilcoxon z=3.58, p=3.5e-4, paired d=0.24. Deliberation beat social influence: d=3.25. Consensus squared log error 0.164 vs 0.195 for the mean of the 3 openers (d=0.40). Individual error after deliberation 0.159 vs 0.230 before (d=0.40).
limits: Small cheap models. One numeric task plus three others. Contradicts the human 'no accuracy gain' finding for LLMs on this task. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: For LLM numeric estimation, showing peers' answers did not hurt accuracy. The cost is diversity (see next line).

source: Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2026) - clone test
finding: Deliberation helped only with model diversity. Three copies of one model deliberating gave no gain over pooling that model's independent estimates.
numbers: Clones: Anthropic z=1.22, p=0.22, d=0.087, BF=5.60 for null; OpenAI z=0.51, p=0.61, d=0.144, BF=3.99; Google z=0.30, p=0.76, d=0.062, BF=6.19. Mixed vs size-matched clones: z=3.61, p=3.1e-4, d=0.48. Convergence in 167 of 168 Study 1 groups.
limits: Moderate Bayesian evidence for the null only. The best single model (Gemini) deliberating with itself beat the mixed consensus (d=0.88), so diversity does not beat one strong model.
agent_relevance: Our attempts come from one model, so they are clones. Talk between them will gain little. Keep them isolated, or diversify the source (prompts, models).

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD?
finding: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling of independent reasoning paths. Debate is sensitive to settings, especially how much agents agree at the start.
numbers: A prompt 'you should agree with the other agents X% of the time' moved Multi-Persona from the worst to the best protocol, beating Medprompt and Self-Consistency (the paper applies a 90% agreement level). Six datasets incl. USMLE.
limits: Exact accuracies sit in figures I did not read. The agreement level was tuned on the benchmark.
agent_relevance: Debate is social influence. Untuned debate lost to independent samples, in line with Lorenz.

source: Hegazy (2024) Diversity of Thought Elicits Stronger Reasoning Capabilities in Multi-Agent Debate Frameworks
finding: Debate across different models beat debate among copies. Mixed medium models after 4 rounds reached 91% on GSM-8K, above GPT-4.
numbers: Gemini-Pro + Mixtral 7Bx8 + PaLM 2-M: 91% on GSM-8K; three Gemini-Pro instances: 82%. ASDiv: 94% for the diverse set.
limits: Single author, modest venue, math benchmarks only. No equal-budget independent-sampling baseline seen in what I read.
agent_relevance: Consistent with the clone result. Diversity of source is what makes social exchange useful.

source: Wu, Song, Yao, Wan, Lin, Lv (2026) DEAR: regulating debate relationships to mitigate blind conformity
finding: States that LLMs in debate show blind conformity: the minority drops independent reasoning to follow the majority. Confidence- or perplexity-based weighting does not fix it and may worsen it.
numbers: Uses two RL agents (who to reference; how to respond). Accuracy numbers not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read. The conformity claim is cited from other work, not measured here.
agent_relevance: Names the same failure as Lorenz for LLM groups. Any peer-visible design needs a guard against majority pull.

source: Douven (2026) Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles
finding: 15 LLMs, 254 prediction-market questions. Learned linear aggregators beat every single model and the classical mean/median. Training-cutoff contamination inflates results.
numbers: The gap between cloud and local models fell from 35.8% to 8.9% on questions that resolved after all training cutoffs. A pure model-disagreement signal was the simplest useful formula.
limits: No manipulation of social influence; independent elicitation only. Serves as the independent-crowd baseline.
agent_relevance: Independent LLM votes work but check for leakage. Disagreement among attempts is itself a usable signal.

source: Older work cited by Lorenz et al. (not opened): Galton 1907; Page diversity prediction theorem; Salganik, Dodds, Watts 2006; Latane social impact theory; French 1956 / DeGroot
finding: Backward citation trail: Galton ox-weight median; the diversity prediction theorem; the artificial music market where visible downloads made hits unpredictable; social impact theory (conformity as a power of group size, exponent below 1); averaging models of opinion.
numbers: Not opened. Latane power-law claim is as summarised in Mavrodiev et al.
limits: Secondary mentions only.
agent_relevance: The formal base for influence models is DeGroot averaging; use for simulations.
